tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ When `execute_code` is available, use it to read Datadog data, even for a single lookup: one script can make several API calls, join data across products, and return only what the answer needs. Skill guides still apply for domain knowledge (query syntax, attribute and metric names, pitfalls), but where a guide tells you to call a specific read tool such as `search_datadog_logs`, `analyze_datadog_logs`, or `get_datadog_metric`, make the equivalent call from `execute_code` instead, using `search_datadog_sdk` to find it. This takes precedence over tool choices in skill guides. Use the named tool only when `search_datadog_sdk` finds no operation for what you need, or when `execute_code` still fails for a step after following its own error guidance. This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

Prioritize skills over tools.

## linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

Tools accept human-readable references, so you rarely need to look up IDs first: issue identifiers such as LIN-123, project identifiers such as P-ENG-12, team names or keys, user names or emails, and "me" for the authenticated user. Only call list_teams, list_users, or similar tools when a reference is ambiguous or unknown.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Statuses and labels belong to teams and differ between them. When you are not sure which values a team supports, call list_issue_statuses or list_issue_labels for that team before filtering or setting them.

get_issue does not include the issue's discussion. Call list_comments with the issue ID to read comments, including inline comments on the description.

Issue descriptions, comments, and documents often embed screenshots and other uploads as markdown images. Pass that markdown to extract_images to view them. Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. A collapsible section opens with +++ followed by its title, and closes with +++ on its own line:

+++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

+++

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

question.description: The question to ask the user

options.description: Up to 4 options for the user to choose from. Do not include 'Other' - it is automatically provided.

header.description: Short label displayed above the question.

multiSelect.description: If true, user can select multiple options. Answers are comma-separated.

tools.name: mcp__linear__get_attachment
tools.description: Retrieve an issue attachment by ID. Use format=url to get its title and download URL without fetching the file content. Linear upload URLs are signed for five minutes; call again to refresh. External URLs are returned unchanged. Files embedded in comments have no issue attachment ID; use the URLs in list_comments attachments instead. Download and process documents with your own file tools.

id.description: Issue attachment ID from get_issue's attachments array (attachments[].id)

format.description: Omit or use content to fetch a Linear-hosted file. Use url for attachment metadata without fetching the file; also supports external links

tools.name: mcp__linear__get_issue
tools.description: Retrieve detailed information about an issue by ID, including attachments, git branch name, and active Triage Intelligence suggestions when the issue is in triage. A nonempty fields selection overrides the include options; request optional fields directly in fields.

id.description: Issue ID or identifier (e.g., LIN-123). P-prefixed identifiers (e.g., P-ENG-123) are projects, not issues

fields.description: Fields to include in each result. Explicitly requested fields with no value return null. `id` is always included. Omit or pass an empty array for the default response.

tools.name: mcp__linear__get_issue_status
tools.description: Retrieve detailed information about an issue status in Linear by name or ID

tools.description: Get a page of notifications from the authenticated user's Linear inbox.

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return per page

cursor.description: Omit for the first page. To continue, pass the previous response's cursor when hasNextPage is true

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ When `execute_code` is available, use it to read Datadog data, even for a single lookup: one script can make several API calls, join data across products, and return only what the answer needs. Skill guides still apply for domain knowledge (query syntax, attribute and metric names, pitfalls), but where a guide tells you to call a specific read tool such as `search_datadog_logs`, `analyze_datadog_logs`, or `get_datadog_metric`, make the equivalent call from `execute_code` instead, using `search_datadog_sdk` to find it. This takes precedence over tool choices in skill guides. Use the named tool only when `search_datadog_sdk` finds no operation for what you need, or when `execute_code` still fails for a step after following its own error guidance. This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

## linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

Tools accept human-readable references, so you rarely need to look up IDs first: issue identifiers such as LIN-123, project identifiers such as P-ENG-12, team names or keys, user names or emails, and "me" for the authenticated user. Only call list_teams, list_users, or similar tools when a reference is ambiguous or unknown.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Statuses and labels belong to teams and differ between them. When you are not sure which values a team supports, call list_issue_statuses or list_issue_labels for that team before filtering or setting them.

get_issue does not include the issue's discussion. Call list_comments with the issue ID to read comments, including inline comments on the description.

Issue descriptions, comments, and documents often embed screenshots and other uploads as markdown images. Pass that markdown to extract_images to view them. Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. A collapsible section opens with +++ followed by its title, and closes with +++ on its own line:

+++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

+++

<total_tokens>14961043 tokens left</total_tokens>

{"id":"COR-2310","uuid":"0370fb5d-4222-4426-9f4f-b1b64e7dc564","title":"Brain: measure what brief's history arm uniquely surfaced; close distill coverage gaps","description":"**Repo:** entireio/entire-brain · **Phase C of the memories-only retrieval decision** (see <issue id="e540d772-0613-4636-a0e3-137441d4668b" label="COR-2307" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2307/brain-brief-precedent-section-from-fact-provenance-anchors-not-history" />)

## Why

Distill is lossy by design: \~263k transcript-derived history records collapse into \~2.8k facts. With history search leaving brief's default path (<issue id="42fefac0-46c9-4341-8538-f9c3a4b3958b" label="COR-2308" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2308/brain-remove-history-search-and-the-raw-scan-from-briefs-default-path" />), anything only the history arm could surface becomes invisible to the default flow. Each such gap is now a distill bug, not a reason to restore a second search system.

## Work

1. **Measure:** replay a representative set of recent brief tasks (the repo's own session history is the corpus) on a build with the old history arm and a memories-only build. Diff the history/precedent sections. Classify every hit the old arm had that the new flow lacks: (a) content also present in a fact the ranking missed → ranking bug (file against the ranking issue), (b) content never distilled → coverage gap, (c) noise (derived-index junk, duplicate copies) → no action.
2. **Decide on mention-grade facts:** for class (b), evaluate a cheap fact kind recording "session X touched identifier/file Y" with locus and anchors, extracted without an extra LLM pass if possible. It must carry its own distill budget — the store at \~2.8k facts is healthy, and mention bloat would degrade recall precision. Rejecting mention-facts and accepting the gap explicitly is a valid outcome; record either decision in Brain with rationale.

## Acceptance

* A written classification of the diff (counts per class, examples).
* Either a mention-grade fact design agreed and filed for implementation, or a recorded decision to accept the gap.","priority":{"value":0,"name":"No priority"},"url":"https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2310/brain-measure-what-briefs-history-arm-uniquely-surfaced-close-distill","gitBranchName":"evis/cor-2310-brain-measure-what-briefs-history-arm-uniquely","createdAt":"2026-11-09T04:57:43.047Z","updatedAt":"2026-11-09T04:57:43.047Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":[],"attachments":[],"documents":[],"stateHistory":[{"state":{"id":"6170bf77-16d7-4d42-9fe6-e0090e8536a0","name":"Backlog","type":"backlog"},"startedAt":"2026-11-09T04:57:43.047Z","endedAt":null}],"createdBy":"Evis Drenova","createdById":"bd1c458e-3bb3-4d0c-8ad7-e36f19afc156","assignee":"Evis Drenova","assigneeId":"bd1c458e-3bb3-4d0c-8ad7-e36f19afc156","team":"Core","teamId":"894690b6-2173-4cbe-abd3-6e7ea5ff5bb9","relations":{"blocks":[],"blockedBy":[],"relatedTo":[{"id":"COR-2307","title":"Brain: brief precedent section from fact provenance anchors, not history search"},{"id":"COR-2308","title":"Brain: remove history search and the raw scan from brief's default path"}],"duplicateOf":null}}

# Historical benchmark archive

This archive records what we tested, what happened, and why some results did not support a claim.
It contains 152 retained records and 48 restored context files, totaling about 12 MB.
Every archived file matches the pre-cleanup snapshot. Positive, negative, invalid, and inconclusive records remain together.

These are historical records, not current product measurements. Old commands and instructions describe the original experiments and must not be treated as current workflows.
The archive has no Python programs, dependencies, or virtual environments. The Go integrity check reads data only.

## Experiment index

| Work | Records and conclusion | Restored context | Limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Agent retrieval comparisons | [Clean comparison series](evidence/semantic-clean-proof/README.md), including earlier and negative comparisons | [Conditions](CONDITIONS.md) and the corresponding [task definitions](tasks/) | The narrow positive comparison measured a complete packet treatment. It did not isolate retrieval alone. |
| Temporal memory and history delivery | [Development pilot and correction](temporal-memory/phase0b-powered-pilot-memo.md), [clean history comparison](evidence/replay-lab-clean/README.md), and [delivery experiments](evidence/history-delivery-fix/README.md) | [Development protocol](temporal-memory/phase0a-development.json), [sealed-smoke protocol](temporal-memory/phase0a-sealed-smoke.json), [source identity](temporal-memory/phase0a-source-artifact.json), tasks, and [comparison configuration](panels/p01-clean-proof-claude.json) | Keep invalid delivery runs, exclusions, and small-sample limitations with the corrected results. Private checkpoint content is not bundled. |
| Distillation scheduling | [Local audit](evidence/distill-perf/distill-perf-audit-report.md) and [larger-repository audit](evidence/distill-perf-large/distill-perf-audit-report.md), with timing records and manifests | Workload and command-agent settings remain in the retained manifests and records | These measure historical local scheduling. They do not establish hosted-model latency or current performance. |
| Packet formats and brief profiling | [Compact v3 measurements](PACKET-FORMAT-V3-LOCAL-MEASUREMENT.md) and [brief profile specification](BRIEF-PROFILE-BASELINE.md) | [Earlier A/B design](PACKET-FORMAT-AB.md), [v2 design](PACKET-FORMAT-V2-AB.md), and [profile corpus identities](brief-profile-corpus-v1.json) | Development measurements do not establish agent quality. The identity snapshot does not include the complete 114-task prompt corpus. |
| Release controls and negative comparisons | [Release evidence](evidence/release/README.md), [facts evaluation](evidence/facts-eval/facts-eval-audit-report.md), [release matrix](evidence/release-matrix/README.md), [Radar tool checks](evidence/radar-tool/README.md), and [workspace checks](evidence/workspace-radar/README.md) | Matching tasks, [comparison configurations](panels/), and four historical Go [scoring fixtures](fixtures/validation/entireio-cli/) | Retain the original no-release-claim decisions. Tool-contract success does not prove agent performance. |
| Confirmatory planning and blocked decisions | [No-go decision](confirmatory/go-no-go.json), [power analysis](confirmatory/power-analysis.json), and [blocked ranking decision](analysis/WORKSTREAM-7-GATE-REPORT-2026-07-15.md) | [Preregistration](confirmatory/PREREGISTRATION.md), [engine matrix](confirmatory/engine-matrix.json), [analyzer identity](confirmatory/analyzer-lock.json), and [power calibration](confirmatory/power-calibration-exploratory-v1.json) | Plans and readiness checks are not completed confirmatory experiments. Larger development corpora and private attestations remain omitted. |
| Exploratory analysis | [Earlier-run analysis](analysis/reports/existing-winner-suites-exploratory.md) and [ranking diagnostic output](analysis/artifacts/ranking-baseline-output-v1.json) | Source identities and methodology remain in the records | Some source suites and synthetic analyzer inputs are not archived. These reports are exploratory. |

The [archive manifest](archive-manifest.json) lists every record, context file, SHA-256 digest, experiment, and selected local dependency.
Its reference lists connect retained outcomes to task definitions, comparison configurations to tasks, and tasks to their scoring fixtures.

## Source and completeness

All 200 historical files come from commit `115f271363804359a195708807435bff7a7136fe`.
This is the archive's source snapshot, not necessarily the revision used for each original run.
Per-run provenance remains authoritative for dates, model versions, source commits, configurations, and recorded hashes.
A restored task definition can differ from an earlier run's recorded configuration hash.

We retain the 24 task definitions named in the recorded outcomes, six comparison configurations, four Go scoring fixtures, and 14 methodology or configuration files.
The scoring fixtures preserve historical success criteria; the current Go tests do not execute them.
Large candidate collections, unused task pools, duplicate snapshots, synthetic analyzer fixtures, and retired runners remain deleted.

This archive supports historical inspection. It is not a complete reproduction bundle.
Historical documents can reference omitted files, retired commands, private data, or external tools.
Use the source commit to inspect omitted tracked files. Git history cannot supply private inputs that were never committed.
Do not interpret historical commands as instructions to reinstall the old tooling.

## Integrity checks

Run the archive checks with Go:

```sh
go test ./tools/releasecheck -run 'TestHistoricalBenchmarkArchive|TestArchiveIntegrity' -count=1
```

The check verifies file hashes, complete inventory, experiment entries, and the manifest's required local references.
It rejects missing, changed, unlisted, or linked files. It does not run historical commands or certify experimental validity.
Normal CI and `mise run check` include this test package.

When intentionally changing the archive, review the source and update the manifest together.
Keep historical records unchanged when adding an interpretation; put the new explanation in this index.
Use `mise run check` for current source checks and `mise run release:readiness` for current local release checks.
--- CONDITIONS
# Entire Brain Benchmark Conditions

This document is the normative contract for Agent Brain benchmarks. It defines
what each agent may see and use, how implementation comparisons must be run,
and what evidence makes a result valid. If another benchmark document is
ambiguous, follow this one and update the drift.

The central comparison is simple:

- **no-Brain** is a normal coding agent with its normal tools, but without
  `entire`, `entire-graph`, `entire-brain`, or any Entire-managed memory.
- **Brain** is the same agent with the same normal tools plus the Brain surface
  selected by the condition.
- **Neither variant may use information from a previous benchmark run.**

Git history is a normal coding tool. `git log`, `git show`, `git blame`,
`git diff`, and other ordinary Git commands are allowed in both variants.
The harness represents its prepared workspace as a synthetic merge whose first
parent has the same tree. Agents must not explicitly diff the synthetic second
parent or request merge-parent patches: that reconstructs harness setup rather
than inspecting ordinary source history.

## Non-negotiable rules

1. Use real coding agents on real repository tasks. Do not replace an agent
   session with a synthetic caller, an internal retriever invocation, or a
   benchmark-specific answer generator.
2. Give both variants the same task, repository state, normal tools, runner,
   model, effort, timeout, and validation.
3. Keep prior benchmark prompts, patches, answers, logs, summaries, worktrees,
   and agent sessions out of both variants.
4. Require the Brain variant to use the configured Brain surface. A row where
   the agent ignores Brain is invalid, even if the patch passes.
5. Keep no-Brain free of every Entire-family tool and every Entire-managed
   memory source.
6. Use current mainline. Entire Brain has no released product baseline, so an
   old checkout or old Brain binary is never an implementation control.
7. Audit the raw agent protocol log. A passing validator or aggregate score
   cannot prove condition compliance.
8. Treat validation pass rate and measured token use as the headline metrics.
   Report wall-clock agent time and the component score, but do not let the
   composite score conceal a validation failure.

## Condition access matrix

| Capability | no-Brain | Brain |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read and edit the task repository | Yes | Yes |
| Shell, source search, builds, tests, and language tools | Yes | Yes |
| Ordinary Git history, including `log`, `show`, and `blame` | Yes | Yes |
| Other normal tools exposed to the agent, including web access | Yes | Yes |
| `entire`, `entire-graph`, or `entire-brain` in any form | **No** | Yes |
| Brain MCP tools | **No** | When selected by the condition |
| Entire checkpoint refs, `.entire`, plugin stores, or derived memory | **No** | Only through the selected Brain surface |
| Files or information from previous benchmark runs | **No** | **No** |
| Host agent conversation/session memory | **No** | **No** |

“Ordinary Git history” means the task repository's source history. It does not
include mining Entire-managed checkpoint refs or reconstructing the Brain
treatment through `.entire` data in a no-Brain run.

# Entire Brain Benchmark Conditions

This document is the normative contract for Agent Brain benchmarks. It defines
what each agent may see and use, how implementation comparisons must be run,
and what evidence makes a result valid. If another benchmark document is
ambiguous, follow this one and update the drift.

The central comparison is simple:

- **no-Brain** is a normal coding agent with its normal tools, but without
  `entire`, `entire-graph`, `entire-brain`, or any Entire-managed memory.
- **Brain** is the same agent with the same normal tools plus the Brain surface
  selected by the condition.
- **Neither variant may use information from a previous benchmark run.**

Git history is a normal coding tool. `git log`, `git show`, `git blame`,
`git diff`, and other ordinary Git commands are allowed in both variants.
The harness represents its prepared workspace as a synthetic merge whose first
parent has the same tree. Agents must not explicitly diff the synthetic second
parent or request merge-parent patches: that reconstructs harness setup rather
than inspecting ordinary source history.

## Non-negotiable rules

1. Use real coding agents on real repository tasks. Do not replace an agent
   session with a synthetic caller, an internal retriever invocation, or a
   benchmark-specific answer generator.
2. Give both variants the same task, repository state, normal tools, runner,
   model, effort, timeout, and validation.
3. Keep prior benchmark prompts, patches, answers, logs, summaries, worktrees,
   and agent sessions out of both variants.
4. Require the Brain variant to use the configured Brain surface. A row where
   the agent ignores Brain is invalid, even if the patch passes.
5. Keep no-Brain free of every Entire-family tool and every Entire-managed
   memory source.
6. Use current mainline. Entire Brain has no released product baseline, so an
   old checkout or old Brain binary is never an implementation control.
7. Audit the raw agent protocol log. A passing validator or aggregate score
   cannot prove condition compliance.
8. Treat validation pass rate and measured token use as the headline metrics.
   Report wall-clock agent time and the component score, but do not let the
   composite score conceal a validation failure.

## Condition access matrix

| Capability | no-Brain | Brain |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read and edit the task repository | Yes | Yes |
| Shell, source search, builds, tests, and language tools | Yes | Yes |
| Ordinary Git history, including `log`, `show`, and `blame` | Yes | Yes |
| Other normal tools exposed to the agent, including web access | Yes | Yes |
| `entire`, `entire-graph`, or `entire-brain` in any form | **No** | Yes |
| Brain MCP tools | **No** | When selected by the condition |
| Entire checkpoint refs, `.entire`, plugin stores, or derived memory | **No** | Only through the selected Brain surface |
| Files or information from previous benchmark runs | **No** | **No** |
| Host agent conversation/session memory | **No** | **No** |

include mining Entire-managed checkpoint refs or reconstructing the Brain
treatment through `.entire` data in a no-Brain run.

#!/bin/sh
# Run one condition, one repetition, against a fresh clone of this repository.
#   run.sh <cond 1-5> <rep> [question-name]        (default question: global-activation)
# Environment:
#   LADDER_OUT=<dir>       where runs land (default: $TMPDIR/memory-ladder-runs). It must be outside this
#                          repository: a clone nested under the source tree would put the un-stripped harness
#                          (rubric, README with results) a relative path away from the agent under test.
#   LADDER_MODEL=<model>   model for the nested agent (default: sonnet)
#   LADDER_ORIGIN=<url>    origin URL to set on the clone (default: this repo's origin). Brain and Graph
#                          derive the repository key from it, so a filesystem path origin breaks them.
#   LADDER_MAX_TURNS=<n>   nested agent turn cap (default: 80)
#   LADDER_BRAIN_BIN=<path> an entire-brain binary to run instead of the installed plugin for conditions 4 and 5
#                          (for example `go build -o /tmp/entire-brain ./cmd/entire-brain` from main). The shim execs it
#                          for `entire brain ...`; it reads the installed store, so no data is relocated. Unset: installed.
#   LADDER_BRANCH=<name>   branch to clone (default: main). Brain scopes facts to the checked-out branch,
#                          so this must be the branch the brain was built for, not the feature branch
#                          you happen to be developing the harness on.
# The nested agent runs read-only and confined to the clone: explicit tool allowlist, no permission
# bypass, no session persistence (see the ALLOW comment below for how each tool is confined).
# Graph prewarm (conditions 3+) is excluded from timing and written to prewarm.txt.
# The clone's HEAD is one commit past the source (the harness directory is stripped), so Brain
# reports its index as one commit behind; its content is unchanged by that commit.
set -eu
COND=${1:-}; REP=${2:-}; Q=${3:-global-activation}
case "$COND" in 1|2|3|4|5) ;; *) echo "cond must be 1-5, got '$COND'" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac
case "$REP" in ''|*[!0-9]*) echo "rep must be a non-negative integer, got '$REP'" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac
case "$Q" in ''|*[!A-Za-z0-9._-]*|.*) echo "question name must match [A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*, got '$Q'" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac
here=$(CDPATH='' cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")" && pwd)
SRC=$(git -C "$here" rev-parse --show-toplevel)
OUT=${LADDER_OUT:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/memory-ladder-runs}
mkdir -p "$OUT"
out_real=$(CDPATH='' cd -- "$OUT" && pwd -P); src_real=$(CDPATH='' cd -- "$SRC" && pwd -P)
case "$out_real/" in "$src_real"/*) echo "LADDER_OUT ($out_real) must be outside the source repository ($src_real): the clone would sit next to the un-stripped harness" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac
ORIGIN=${LADDER_ORIGIN:-$(git -C "$SRC" remote get-url origin)}
BRANCH=${LADDER_BRANCH:-main}
RUN=$OUT/$Q/c${COND}-r${REP}
[ -f "$here/guides/cond${COND}.md" ] || { echo "guides missing; run setup-guides.sh first" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$here/questions/$Q.txt" ] || { echo "unknown question $Q" >&2; exit 1; }
rm -rf "$RUN"; mkdir -p "$RUN"
# Single-branch, non-local clone: the source repository carries Entire's checkpoint refs
# (entire/checkpoints/v1 and entire/<sha>), whose commits hold session transcripts, including
# those of sessions that built or ran this harness. A default clone copies every ref and pack,
# so `git log --all` or `git grep <pat> origin/entire/checkpoints/v1` would hand session
# history, and the answer key quoted inside it, to every condition including "code and git
# only". --single-branch fetches only $BRANCH and tags; --no-local transfers objects as a pack
# instead of hard-linking the source's, so the checkpoint objects are absent, not merely
# unreferenced (measured: 60 MB and 2 s against 600 MB for the default clone).
git clone -q --no-local --single-branch --branch "$BRANCH" "$SRC" "$RUN/repo"
cd "$RUN/repo"
git remote set-url origin "$ORIGIN"
# The agent under test must not be able to read its own grading rubric, the prompt, or the README
# that narrates earlier results. Remove the harness from the worktree and from HEAD's tree, so
# neither the filesystem nor `git show HEAD:...` can reach it. Older history is still reachable
# through git; the strip commit is recorded in summary.json so a reader can check for leakage.
if [ -d benchmarks/memory-ladder ]; then
  git rm -r -q --cached benchmarks/memory-ladder && rm -rf benchmarks/memory-ladder
  git -c user.name=ladder -c user.email=ladder@invalid commit -q -m "memory-ladder: strip harness from the clone under test"
fi
git rev-parse HEAD > "$RUN/head.txt"
cp "$here/guides/cond${COND}.md" CLAUDE.md
rm -f .entire/agent-guide.md
[ "$COND" = 1 ] && rm -f .claude/agents/entire-search.md
export PATH="$here/bin:$PATH" LADDER_COND=$COND
if [ -n "${LADDER_BRAIN_BIN:-}" ] && [ "$COND" -ge 4 ]; then
  [ -x "$LADDER_BRAIN_BIN" ] || { echo "LADDER_BRAIN_BIN is not executable: $LADDER_BRAIN_BIN" >&2; exit 2; }
  export LADDER_BRAIN_BIN
  (cd "$RUN/repo" && entire brain version) > "$RUN/brain_version.txt" 2>&1 || true
fi
if [ "$COND" -ge 3 ]; then
  s=$(date +%s); entire graph index --repo . --profile full >"$RUN/prewarm.log" 2>&1 || true
  echo "prewarm_s=$(( $(date +%s) - s ))" > "$RUN/prewarm.txt"
fi
# Tool confinement, measured against this runtime (see README):
#  - Bash: Claude Code sandboxes file commands to the working directory, so cat/find/ls/grep on a
#    path outside the clone are blocked by the runtime itself.
#  - Read: unconfined by default, so it is granted only under the clone with Read(./**).
#  - Grep and Glob tools: not path-scoped by permission rules, so they are not granted; the agent
#    uses grep, rg, find and ls through the sandboxed shell instead.
#  - Agent (subagents): launches regardless of the allowlist and cannot be scoped to one subagent
#    type by a rule, so it is denied outright below. Subagents did inherit the parent's rules when
#    measured, and no run so far launched one, so this changes nothing in the recorded results.
ALLOW="Read(./**) Bash(cd:*) Bash(git:*) Bash(entire:*) Bash(grep:*) Bash(rg:*) Bash(ls:*) Bash(cat:*) Bash(head:*) Bash(tail:*) Bash(sed -n:*) Bash(find:*) Bash(wc:*) Bash(go doc:*)"
start=$(date +%s)
claude -p "$(cat "$here/questions/$Q.txt")" --model "${LADDER_MODEL:-sonnet}" --output-format stream-json --verbose \
  --setting-sources project --no-session-persistence --max-turns "${LADDER_MAX_TURNS:-80}" \
  --allowedTools "$ALLOW" --disallowedTools "Edit Write MultiEdit NotebookEdit WebFetch WebSearch Agent Task" \
  > "$RUN/stream.jsonl" 2> "$RUN/stderr.log" || echo "exit=$?" > "$RUN/failed.txt"
echo "wall_s=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))" > "$RUN/wall.txt"
LADDER_SRC="$src_real" LADDER_OUT_ROOT="$out_real" python3 "$here/parse.py" "$RUN" > "$RUN/summary.json"
echo "done $Q c${COND}-r${REP}"

LADDER_SRC="$src_real" LADDER_OUT_ROOT="$out_real" python3 "$here/parse.py" "$RUN" > "$RUN/summary.json"
echo "done $Q c${COND}-r${REP}"

#!/bin/sh
# Generate the per-condition CLAUDE.md guides from the product's own output so
# checked-in copies cannot go stale. Writes guides/cond1.md .. cond5.md.
#   cond1  plain repository note, no Entire tooling
#   cond2  plain note + session-history section
#   cond3  `entire graph agent-guide` outside a repository (standalone Graph) + sessions
#   cond4  Brain's `agent-guide --normal` inside this repository (combined Graph and Brain, normal mode,
#          rendered by LADDER_BRAIN_BIN when set so a build under test is what the agent reads) + sessions
#   cond5  this repository's .entire/agent-guide.md as committed (strict if setup --strict was run) + sessions
set -eu
here=$(CDPATH='' cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")" && pwd)
repo=$(git -C "$here" rev-parse --show-toplevel)
out=$here/guides; mkdir -p "$out"
sessions='

## Session history

Previous agent sessions, checkpoints and commits for this repository are
searchable. Use them when a question concerns previous work, decisions, or
history. Always pass --json to search; without it the command opens a TUI.

    entire search "<query>" --json              # checkpoints, commits and sessions
    entire search "<query>" --json --compact    # trimmed output for agents
    entire checkpoint list                      # checkpoints on this branch
    entire checkpoint explain <id|sha>          # explain a checkpoint or commit
    entire checkpoint explain <id|sha> --full   # include the session transcript

Run `entire agent-help <command>` for exact flags.
'
plain='# Repository guide

This is the entire-brain Go repository. Use the source tree and git history
(git log, git blame, git show) to answer questions.'
printf '%s No Entire tooling (session\nhistory, code graph, or brain) is available in this environment.\n' "$plain" > "$out/cond1.md"
printf '%s%s' "$plain" "$sessions" > "$out/cond2.md"
{ (cd / && entire graph agent-guide); printf '%s' "$sessions"; } > "$out/cond3.md"
brain_guide() { if [ -n "${LADDER_BRAIN_BIN:-}" ]; then "$LADDER_BRAIN_BIN" agent-guide --normal --repo "$repo"; else (cd "$repo" && entire brain agent-guide --normal); fi; }
{ brain_guide; printf '%s' "$sessions"; } > "$out/cond4.md"
if [ -f "$repo/.entire/agent-guide.md" ]; then
  { cat "$repo/.entire/agent-guide.md"; printf '%s' "$sessions"; } > "$out/cond5.md"
else
  echo "warning: $repo/.entire/agent-guide.md missing; cond5 falls back to cond4" >&2; cp "$out/cond4.md" "$out/cond5.md"
fi
for c in 3 4; do grep -q "^# Entire repository agent guide" "$out/cond$c.md" || { echo "cond$c guide did not render; is entire graph installed?" >&2; exit 1; }; done
wc -l "$out"/cond*.md

#!/bin/sh
# Condition-gated shim for the Entire CLI, placed first on PATH by run.sh.
#   LADDER_COND=1  no Entire tooling
#   LADDER_COND=2  hosted sessions only (search, checkpoint)
#   LADDER_COND=3  sessions + Graph
#   LADDER_COND=4  sessions + Graph + Brain (normal guide)
#   LADDER_COND=5  sessions + Graph + Brain (strict guide)
# Lifecycle hooks are swallowed so a nested agent run never captures a checkpoint.
sub=${1:-}
case "$sub" in hooks) exit 0 ;; esac
# Drop this shim's own directory from PATH, then resolve the real CLI from what remains, so the
# real binary is found wherever it is installed and its children cannot loop back here.
shimdir=$(CDPATH='' cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")" && pwd)
PATH=$(printf '%s' "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | grep -vx -- "$shimdir" | paste -sd: -); export PATH
REAL=${LADDER_REAL_ENTIRE:-$(command -v entire 2>/dev/null || true)}
[ -n "$REAL" ] && [ -x "$REAL" ] || { echo "entire shim: real entire CLI not found on PATH; set LADDER_REAL_ENTIRE=/path/to/entire" >&2; exit 127; }
deny() { echo "entire: '$sub' is not available in this environment" >&2; exit 1; }
case "${LADDER_COND:-1}" in
  1) echo "entire: command not found" >&2; exit 127 ;;
  2) case "$sub" in search|checkpoint|cp|checkpoints|agent-help|version|status|why) exec "$REAL" "$@" ;; *) deny ;; esac ;;
  3) case "$sub" in search|checkpoint|cp|checkpoints|agent-help|version|status|why|graph) exec "$REAL" "$@" ;; *) deny ;; esac ;;
  4|5)
    case "$sub" in search|checkpoint|cp|checkpoints|agent-help|version|status|why|graph|brain) ;; *) deny ;; esac
    # A build under test replaces the installed Brain plugin for `entire brain ...` only.
    if [ "$sub" = brain ] && [ -n "${LADDER_BRAIN_BIN:-}" ]; then shift; exec "$LADDER_BRAIN_BIN" "$@"; fi
    exec "$REAL" "$@" ;;
  *) echo "entire shim: bad LADDER_COND '${LADDER_COND}'" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
--- run-all
#!/bin/sh
# Run every condition sequentially for N repetitions (arms are not run in parallel so they do not
# contend for the hosted search service, the Brain store or the Graph cache).
#   run-all.sh [reps=3] [question=global-activation] [conditions="1 2 3 4 5"]
set -eu

author:	karthik-rameshkumar
association:	member
edited:	false

--
Two mechanism notes from working on the fix, so the remaining item has a concrete starting point. PR #337 covers the brief ordering and the guide text.

**Why `query` returned only docs.** It is the hybrid fusion structure, not fact scoring. For the same question, `query --keyword` returns 4 doc / 3 fact / 3 history with the decisive fact at rank 2. In hybrid mode, `retrieveUnifiedWithOptions` appends two lists for docs (lexical and vector) and, when the gated embedder is present, two for history, while facts arrive as one already-fused list from `rankFactsFused`. Global RRF then gives a source with two lists up to double the mass of a source with one. The history fusion was designed and measured that way (the +13% useful/1k result), so a fix should weight lists per source or fuse docs internally the way facts are fused, and it needs the retrieval eval pack regenerated first per the recorded convention.

**Self-echo in brief history.** After an agent's own transcripts about a topic are ingested, the brief's history matches for that topic can be entirely that agent's tool-call echoes (`entire brain brief ...`, `entire graph query ...`), displacing the session that holds the decision. The self-echo filter in `query` drops `entire brain` echoes; it does not drop `entire graph` echoes, and the brief's history arm appears to apply neither. Any agent that works on a topic pollutes the next brief on that topic with its own command lines.

--
author:	karthik-rameshkumar
association:	member
edited:	false
status:	none
--
Re-ran the ladder after #337 merged, with Brain built from `main` and a new question whose recorded rejection had not been discussed in any recent session (the first question had been, by then). Same setup as before: fresh clone per run, Sonnet, read-only tools, three repetitions.

| Condition | Recovered the recorded decision and its reason | Mean input tokens |
|---|---|---|
| code + git only | 0/3 | 179k |
| + hosted sessions | 0/3 | 213k |
| + Graph | 0/3 | 224k |
| + Brain, normal guide | **3/3** | 160k |
| + Brain, strict guide | **3/3** | 260k |

Every normal-guide Brain run called `recall` as its first command (the new guide text) and cited the fact with its session, checkpoint and transcript line. Sessions-only runs found the right session through hosted search and explained five other checkpoints from it, but not the one carrying the measurement, which sits at line ~14,000 of a 16,541-line transcript; none read a transcript with `--full`. Two of three strict-guide runs still truncated the brief, but the facts section now lands inside the first 6 KB and one call to `recall` closed the gap.

So the two shipped fixes resolve the agent-visible defect. Remaining item from the original report: `query` in hybrid mode still returns only `doc` results for natural phrasings (docs contribute two RRF lists, facts one); the guide now steers agents to `recall` instead, which is a workaround rather than a fix.

Harness and both runs are in PR #336 (`benchmarks/memory-ladder`).

--
author:	Beehtrix
association:	contributor
edited:	false
status:	none
--
Both defects are addressed. #337 (v0.2.0) moved facts and history ahead of status in `brief --json` and named `recall` in both guides, which your Oct 7 re-run confirmed. The `query` item that kept this open went away soon after: v0.2.0 also removed embedding retrieval (#416), so BM25 is the only ranking and docs no longer get two RRF lists against the facts' one. @karthik-rameshkumar, does a natural-phrasing `query` surface the fact for you now? If it does, this can be closed. One small leftover from your Oct 6 comment: the history self-echo filter still drops only `entire brain` tool calls, not `entire graph` ones.

--

#!/bin/sh
# Run one condition, one repetition, against a fresh clone of this repository.
#   run.sh <cond 1-5> <rep> [question-name]        (default question: global-activation)
# Environment:
#   LADDER_OUT=<dir>       where runs land (default: $TMPDIR/memory-ladder-runs). It must be outside this
#                          repository: a clone nested under the source tree would put the un-stripped harness
#                          (rubric, README with results) a relative path away from the agent under test.
#   LADDER_MODEL=<model>   model for the nested agent (default: sonnet)
#   LADDER_ORIGIN=<url>    origin URL to set on the clone (default: this repo's origin). Brain and Graph
#                          derive the repository key from it, so a filesystem path origin breaks them.
#   LADDER_MAX_TURNS=<n>   nested agent turn cap (default: 80)
#   LADDER_BRAIN_BIN=<path> an entire-brain binary to run instead of the installed plugin for conditions 4 and 5
#                          (for example `go build -o /tmp/entire-brain ./cmd/entire-brain` from main). The shim execs it
#                          for `entire brain ...`; it reads the installed store, so no data is relocated. Unset: installed.
#   LADDER_BRANCH=<name>   branch to clone (default: main). Brain scopes facts to the checked-out branch,
#                          so this must be the branch the brain was built for, not the feature branch
#                          you happen to be developing the harness on.
# The nested agent runs read-only and confined to the clone: explicit tool allowlist, no permission
# bypass, no session persistence (see the ALLOW comment below for how each tool is confined).
# Graph prewarm (conditions 3+) is excluded from timing and written to prewarm.txt.
# The clone's HEAD is one commit past the source (the harness directory is stripped), so Brain
# reports its index as one commit behind; its content is unchanged by that commit.
set -eu
COND=${1:-}; REP=${2:-}; Q=${3:-global-activation}
case "$COND" in 1|2|3|4|5) ;; *) echo "cond must be 1-5, got '$COND'" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac
case "$REP" in ''|*[!0-9]*) echo "rep must be a non-negative integer, got '$REP'" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac
case "$Q" in ''|*[!A-Za-z0-9._-]*|.*) echo "question name must match [A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*, got '$Q'" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac
here=$(CDPATH='' cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")" && pwd)
SRC=$(git -C "$here" rev-parse --show-toplevel)
OUT=${LADDER_OUT:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/memory-ladder-runs}
mkdir -p "$OUT"
out_real=$(CDPATH='' cd -- "$OUT" && pwd -P); src_real=$(CDPATH='' cd -- "$SRC" && pwd -P)
case "$out_real/" in "$src_real"/*) echo "LADDER_OUT ($out_real) must be outside the source repository ($src_real): the clone would sit next to the un-stripped harness" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac
ORIGIN=${LADDER_ORIGIN:-$(git -C "$SRC" remote get-url origin)}
BRANCH=${LADDER_BRANCH:-main}
RUN=$OUT/$Q/c${COND}-r${REP}
[ -f "$here/guides/cond${COND}.md" ] || { echo "guides missing; run setup-guides.sh first" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$here/questions/$Q.txt" ] || { echo "unknown question $Q" >&2; exit 1; }
rm -rf "$RUN"; mkdir -p "$RUN"
# Single-branch, non-local clone: the source repository carries Entire's checkpoint refs
# (entire/checkpoints/v1 and entire/<sha>), whose commits hold session transcripts, including
# those of sessions that built or ran this harness. A default clone copies every ref and pack,
# so `git log --all` or `git grep <pat> origin/entire/checkpoints/v1` would hand session
# history, and the answer key quoted inside it, to every condition including "code and git
# only". --single-branch fetches only $BRANCH and tags; --no-local transfers objects as a pack
# instead of hard-linking the source's, so the checkpoint objects are absent, not merely
# unreferenced (measured: 60 MB and 2 s against 600 MB for the default clone).
git clone -q --no-local --single-branch --branch "$BRANCH" "$SRC" "$RUN/repo"
cd "$RUN/repo"
git remote set-url origin "$ORIGIN"
# The agent under test must not be able to read its own grading rubric, the prompt, or the README
# that narrates earlier results. Remove the harness from the worktree and from HEAD's tree, so
# neither the filesystem nor `git show HEAD:...` can reach it. Older history is still reachable
# through git; the strip commit is recorded in summary.json so a reader can check for leakage.
if [ -d benchmarks/memory-ladder ]; then
  git rm -r -q --cached benchmarks/memory-ladder && rm -rf benchmarks/memory-ladder
  git -c user.name=ladder -c user.email=ladder@invalid commit -q -m "memory-ladder: strip harness from the clone under test"
fi
git rev-parse HEAD > "$RUN/head.txt"
cp "$here/guides/cond${COND}.md" CLAUDE.md
rm -f .entire/agent-guide.md
[ "$COND" = 1 ] && rm -f .claude/agents/entire-search.md
export PATH="$here/bin:$PATH" LADDER_COND=$COND
if [ -n "${LADDER_BRAIN_BIN:-}" ] && [ "$COND" -ge 4 ]; then
  [ -x "$LADDER_BRAIN_BIN" ] || { echo "LADDER_BRAIN_BIN is not executable: $LADDER_BRAIN_BIN" >&2; exit 2; }
  export LADDER_BRAIN_BIN
  (cd "$RUN/repo" && entire brain version) > "$RUN/brain_version.txt" 2>&1 || true
fi
if [ "$COND" -ge 3 ]; then
  s=$(date +%s); entire graph index --repo . --profile full >"$RUN/prewarm.log" 2>&1 || true
  echo "prewarm_s=$(( $(date +%s) - s ))" > "$RUN/prewarm.txt"
fi
# Tool confinement, measured against this runtime (see README):
#  - Bash: Claude Code sandboxes file commands to the working directory, so cat/find/ls/grep on a
#    path outside the clone are blocked by the runtime itself.
#  - Read: unconfined by default, so it is granted only under the clone with Read(./**).
#  - Grep and Glob tools: not path-scoped by permission rules, so they are not granted; the agent
#    uses grep, rg, find and ls through the sandboxed shell instead.
#  - Agent (subagents): launches regardless of the allowlist and cannot be scoped to one subagent
#    type by a rule, so it is denied outright below. Subagents did inherit the parent's rules when
#    measured, and no run so far launched one, so this changes nothing in the recorded results.
ALLOW="Read(./**) Bash(cd:*) Bash(git:*) Bash(entire:*) Bash(grep:*) Bash(rg:*) Bash(ls:*) Bash(cat:*) Bash(head:*) Bash(tail:*) Bash(sed -n:*) Bash(find:*) Bash(wc:*) Bash(go doc:*)"
start=$(date +%s)
claude -p "$(cat "$here/questions/$Q.txt")" --model "${LADDER_MODEL:-sonnet}" --output-format stream-json --verbose \
  --setting-sources project --no-session-persistence --max-turns "${LADDER_MAX_TURNS:-80}" \
  --allowedTools "$ALLOW" --disallowedTools "Edit Write MultiEdit NotebookEdit WebFetch WebSearch Agent Task" \
  > "$RUN/stream.jsonl" 2> "$RUN/stderr.log" || echo "exit=$?" > "$RUN/failed.txt"
echo "wall_s=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))" > "$RUN/wall.txt"
LADDER_SRC="$src_real" LADDER_OUT_ROOT="$out_real" python3 "$here/parse.py" "$RUN" > "$RUN/summary.json"
echo "done $Q c${COND}-r${REP}"

"""Summarise runs for one question: per-run metrics, rubric hits, and per-condition means.

    python3 grade.py [question=global-activation] [--json]

Rubric regexes come from questions/<question>.rubric.json; 'recovered' is a first pass
and should be hand-checked against the answers in runs/<question>/*/summary.json.
"""
import glob, json, os, re, statistics, sys

here = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
q = next((a for a in sys.argv[1:] if not a.startswith("--")), "global-activation")

---
name: entire-brain-local-install-layout
description: "Where the real entire-brain watcher, plugin binary, state, and logs live on this machine"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: ed978183-a7b6-439d-9fed-9f65f93af2c6
  modified: 2026-11-06T23:01:02.309Z
---

On this machine the canonical entire-brain plugin binary is
`~/.local/share/entire/plugins/bin/entire-brain`, a symlink to
`~/.local/bin/entire-brain` — since 2026-10-23 that target is a REAL binary
(a dev build as of 2026-10-26), not a symlink into a repo checkout. To run a
dev build through `entire brain`, overwrite that file:
`go build -o ~/.local/bin/entire-brain ./cmd/entire-brain`. The old layout
(symlink into /Users/evisdrenova/conductor/repos/entire-brain) is gone.

Breakage mode seen 2026-10-26: something re-pointed the plugins/bin symlink at
a Conductor workspace build (`conductor/workspaces/entire-brain/miami/...`);
the workspace was deleted and every `entire brain` call failed with "points at
a file that no longer exists". Fix: `ln -sf ~/.local/bin/entire-brain
~/.local/share/entire/plugins/bin/entire-brain`. Never symlink the plugin at
an ephemeral workspace path. Note the brain store manifest is schema 4 now;
binaries built from main older than ~2026-10-21 only read schema 3 and fail
with memory_unsupported_version.

RESOLVED 2026-11-06: the installed binary had been built from an Oct 26 commit
predating the proposal-framework removal (PR #587), the MCP removal, and the
flat fact store, causing phantom `proposals: 59329`, an `mcp` feature, a
176-dir per-branch store (24,735 lines for ~2,834 unique facts), and false
staleness warnings. Fixed by rebuilding from main c1d42ec0 into
~/.local/bin/entire-brain (backup: entire-brain.bak-20261106) and running
`entire brain refresh --agent none`: store migrated to flat facts/store.json
(2,827 facts), proposals/branches 0, freshness ok. Lesson: most brain warning
noise here = stale installed binary; rebuild + refresh before debugging.
Still open: the brain is keyed by origin remote and shared across Conductor
worktrees, so "seed is stale" can recur (seed matches at most one worktree's
HEAD); the watcher defers full refresh while the worktree is dirty, so in
Conductor it effectively never runs; pattern-layer refresh step fails
non-fatally on one >256MB transcript (fix-brain-nosessions-loop-38ee254b).

The launchd watcher label is `io.entire.brain-watch.a2d3fd66` (plist in
`~/Library/LaunchAgents/`). State dir is `~/.local/state/entire/`
(watch-plan.json, logs/watch.log); brain data under
`~/.local/share/entire/plugins/data/brain/repos/`.

Repaired 2026-10-20: the registration had pointed at a deleted
`/tmp/eb-validate/entire-brain` (EX_CONFIG crash loop); fixed with the binary's
`daemon-reregister` command (added by PR #420). If the daemon wedges again,
run `<plugin-bin> daemon-reregister` — no token spend, rewrites the unit and
bootout/enable/bootstraps under the registration lock.
