tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

input.body:
Parity gate run and **passed** — the memories-only brief does not just match plain session search, it beats it on both ladder questions, at roughly a quarter to half the input tokens.

## Defect confirmation (step 1)

Both recorded defects are fixed on main (0f898ab4):
- Brief layout (#335): `brief --json` orders facts → precedent → guidance → status; no history section.
- Guide command: both guides name `recall` for prior decisions and frame transcript search (`query --source history`) as explicit escalation; wording is pinned by an integration test since COR-2308.

## Method

- Harness: the deleted memory-ladder harness restored from git history (`4bbd2e8b^`), run untracked; nothing recommitted. Conditions 2 (plain note + hosted session search), 4 (Brain normal guide + sessions), 5 (strict committed guide + sessions); 3 repetitions; both questions; Sonnet; fresh single-branch clone per run pinned to origin/main; Brain binary for conditions 4/5 built from main (`LADDER_BRAIN_BIN`).
- Harness repairs were needed before any valid run — the resurrected git shim predates Brain's current git invocation style and silently rewired Brain to an empty store (every read said "no brain has been built"): strip benign git globals (`--no-optional-locks -c …`) before dispatch, allow read-only `git remote`, allow `git config` reads by flag scan. Recorded in Brain as `fact:8ca669d85e628251f01725dc`. The first full matrix ran before the diagnosis and was discarded.
- All 18 runs completed. 9 were auto-flagged "contaminated"; re-audit found **zero content-marker hits** (no rubric text, no results tables). The flags were hosted-search listing rows naming the `bench/memory-ladder-harness` branch and one precedent excerpt showing the question text being authored — text the agent already has. Attempts to open the benchmark session via `entire checkpoint explain` returned empty (checkpoint refs are absent from the single-branch clone). All runs were therefore graded, with this amendment disclosed.

## Results — recorded decision + its reason recovered (hand-checked)

| Condition | global-activation | test-first-checklist | mean input tokens (GA / TFC) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2: plain session search | 0/3 (one run found the policy via docs, without the recorded reason; two said "no evidence found") | 0/3 (all found the opt-in default; none the measured reason) | 528k / 501k |
| 4: Brain normal, memories-only brief | **3/3** | **3/3** | 148k / 131k |
| 5: Brain strict guide | **3/3** | **3/3** | 239k / 273k |

All 12 Brain runs cited the decisive fact id (`fact:8e10b73c…` for global activation; the measured 31%-tokens/27%-time rejection for the checklist question), most with session/checkpoint anchors. Wall-clock durations are omitted: the final 16 runs executed 8-way parallel, so they are contention-noisy.

Two context points:
- Versus the Oct 7 re-run (history arm still in brief): Brain normal was 3/3 at ~160k mean tokens; memories-only is 3/3 at ~131–148k. Removing the history arm cost nothing on this gate.
- Plain session search fell from 3/3 (Oct 6, question 1) to 0/3 now: the hosted corpus has grown by a month of sessions (including the benchmark's own), and the decisive transcript lines no longer surface. The sessions arm degrades as the corpus grows; the memories arm did not.

## Acceptance

- Parity reached (exceeded) — no distill or ranking bugs to file: there were no Brain misses. COR-2311 stays motivated by its own evidence, not by this gate.
- Caveat: n=3 per cell, two questions, one repo, both questions discussed in prior sessions (which this time could only help the sessions arm, since clones cannot open checkpoint content).

Parity result recorded in Brain as `fact:952847dcff2f08b32389f83a`. Run artifacts and the amended grading audit are in the workspace (`$TMPDIR/eb-ladder`, `.context/cor2309-linear-comment.md`).

**Condition 4 — Brain, normal guide.** Adds Brain with the memories-only brief (built from main) plus the normal agent guide. Tests the new default path: brief, then `recall`. This is the surface COR-2308 shipped.
Result: **3/3 and 3/3.** Mean input: ~131–148k tokens. Every run cited the exact fact id for the decision.

content.text:
Yes. The Brain conditions (4 and 5) ran a binary built from current main: the brief has no history search and no raw scan. It serves facts, plus the precedent section built from each fact's provenance anchors (session, checkpoint, transcript line, commit). History search exists only as the opt-in escalation — and no run needed it.

What the results tell us:

1. **The removal was safe.** The history arm was kept as a safety net because the facts path was not trusted. With it gone, recovery did not drop: 12/12, same as the October run that still had the arm, and at slightly fewer tokens.

2. **Distilled facts are the better retrieval surface, not just an equal one.** Every Brain run got the decision from one `recall` or brief hit and cited the fact id. The sessions arm had the same information available in raw transcripts and found it 0/6.

3. **Provenance anchors do the job the history section used to do.** Agents cited session and checkpoint ids from the precedent anchors. A lookup from the winning fact replaces a second search.

4. **Raw session search gets worse as the corpus grows.** It was 3/3 in October on question 1 and is 0/6 now. The decisive lines sink deeper as sessions accumulate. Facts do not sink: distill keeps one durable record. This means session search is also no longer a trustworthy gold baseline for future comparisons.

5. **It is much cheaper.** ~131–148k mean input tokens versus ~500–530k for session search — about 4x less context spent for a better answer.

Caveats: n=3 per cell, two questions, one repo. Strong enough to close the gate; not a general benchmark claim.

content.text:
The n=15 matrix is running: 90 runs (2 questions × 3 conditions × 15 reps), 8-way parallel, expected 30–45 minutes.

**Methodology review — what the eval does and what I changed:**

Sound parts, kept as-is:
- Fresh clone per run; `--single-branch --no-local` keeps checkpoint refs (which contain the answer transcripts) out of every condition's reach.
- The harness is stripped from the clone's worktree and HEAD; a shimmed read-only git closes the history paths to it; the entire shim gates subcommands per condition.
- Same model (Sonnet), same turn cap, same read-only tool allowlist, no subagents, no session persistence; guides rendered from the product so they cannot go stale.
- Leakage is audited on both tool inputs and tool outputs; contaminated runs are excluded from grading, not patched up.

Weaknesses found and fixed before spending 90 runs:
1. **Contamination rule was source-blind.** Any tool result containing "memory-ladder"/"rubric" contaminated the run. That was right when the only source of those words was the harness; now the benchmark itself lives in the hosted session corpus and the fact store, so `entire` results legitimately mention it. New rule, codified in parse.py: content markers (rubric text, results tables) contaminate from any source; bare word mentions contaminate only in local-reader output (git, cat), and in `entire` results they are recorded as probes instead. All harness tests pass, including the ones that pin the strict git behavior.
2. **Durations are contention-noisy under parallelism** — tokens and recovery are the reported metrics.
3. **n=3 was thin** — now 15 per cell.

Known limits that remain (disclosed, not fixable here): two questions, one repo; the `recovered` grade is regex-plus-hand-check, so I will hand-check the surprising cells; the hosted search corpus is live, so condition 2 is a moving baseline — that is itself one of the findings.

I will grade and report when the matrix finishes.

input.body:
Re-ran at **n=15 per cell** (90 runs, 8-way parallel, same harness and build) after a methodology review. Gate conclusion unchanged and now firm.

Methodology changes before the run, codified in the harness: the contamination rule is now source-aware — content markers (rubric text, results tables) contaminate from any source; bare harness-word mentions contaminate only in local-reader output (git/cat), while `entire` results carrying them (hosted listings and store facts legitimately name the benchmark now) are recorded as probes. Harness tests pass. Durations are not reported (parallel contention); recovery and tokens are the metrics.

## Results — recorded decision + reason recovered (regex + hand-check of every borderline)

| Condition | global-activation | test-first-checklist | combined | mean input tokens (GA / TFC) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2: plain session search | 2/13 | 0/15 | **2/28 (7%)** | 612k / 602k |
| 4: Brain normal, memories-only brief | 13/15 | 15/15 | **28/30 (93%)** | 249k / 138k |
| 5: Brain strict guide | 15/15 | 15/15 | **30/30** | 379k / 284k |

- All 90 runs completed. 2 c2 runs were excluded as genuinely contaminated: hosted search served benchmark-session content (one content-marker hit each). The local clone cannot reach it; the hosted corpus can.
- Hand-grading corrections applied: one c2 regex hit was a false positive (the answer explicitly denied a prior attempt — graded miss); two c2 hits are genuine (one cites the decision session directly).

## The two c4 misses (per the gate protocol: misses become distill/ranking bugs)

Both misses retrieved **sibling facts** from the same decision family (the activation-recorded-in-guide-file invariant `fact:1de812d5…`, the consent rationale) but not the decisive closed-negative (`fact:8e10b73c…`); one concluded "no recorded decision" while the fact exists. The fact is in the store and 13 other phrasings retrieved it, so this is not a distill coverage gap — it is recall ranking among related facts. Filed as a data point on COR-2311 (related_ids collapse / ranking quality), not a new issue.

Observations:
- The strict guide went 30/30 vs normal 28/30, at ~1.5–2x the tokens. The extra directives buy retrieval persistence.
- Plain session search is now 2/28 on questions it once answered 3/3; the moving hosted corpus keeps burying the decisive lines. It is not a usable gold baseline for future retrieval comparisons on this repo.

Benchmark data point from the COR-2309 parity gate (n=15 per cell, memories-only brief, main build):

2 of 15 Brain normal-guide runs on the global-activation question missed the decisive closed-negative `fact:8e10b73c…` ("tried and reverted because it activated Brain in repositories where the user had never enabled it"). Both instead retrieved sibling facts from the same decision family — `fact:1de812d5…` (activation is recorded in the guide file, does not probe plugins) and the consent-rationale fact — and one concluded "no recorded decision" while the fact exists. 13 other phrasings ranked it correctly, and the strict guide went 15/15, so this is recall ranking among related facts, not distill coverage.

This is a concrete instance of the related_ids collapse problem this issue tracks: when siblings of one decision family fill the top slots, the closed-negative that answers "was this tried before" can be displaced by its own context facts. Run artifacts: `$TMPDIR/eb-ladder-n15/global-activation/c4-r9` and `c4-r10` in the san-jose workspace.

content.text:
**The memories-only architecture is validated. Ship-and-move-on.**

1. **Removing history search from the brief was the right call.** With 90 runs of evidence: distilled facts + provenance anchors recover recorded decisions 93–100% of the time; the raw-transcript search they replaced manages 7%. The safety net wasn't protecting anything — it was mostly re-serving noise (86% of what it surfaced) and content the facts already carry.

2. **Distill is the load-bearing step, and it is holding.** No coverage gaps worth fixing: the 4% the history arm uniquely surfaced is ephemeral session narration, reachable on demand through the opt-in escalation. No mention-grade fact kind needed.

3. **The one real weakness is ranking among related facts** (2/30 misses where sibling facts displaced the decisive closed-negative, once producing a false "no record exists"). That's COR-2311, and it now has concrete failure artifacts to work from. A false "none found" is the worst failure mode for a memory system, so that issue deserves priority.

4. **Two durable side-lessons:** raw session search degrades as the corpus grows, so stop treating it as the gold baseline for retrieval evals on this repo; and the strict guide trades ~1.5–2x tokens for 30/30 persistence — a knob, not a default.

Both tickets are complete; statuses are yours to flip. Next concrete work, if you want it: COR-2311.

## Why

With memories as the only default retrieval surface, recall-time ranking quality carries the whole load. The 2026-11-06 retrieval audit found three concrete issues:

1. **Unresolved near-duplicates reach recall:** when distill judges two facts related below the old confidence threshold, both stay active cross-linked via `related_ids` (`factmerge/merge.go:40-46`). \~1,910 active records carry `related_ids`; pairs surface as separate results. Collapse linked facts into one result at recall time (newest or highest-scored wins, others listed as alternates). Complementary to <issue id="e6be68d8-58ee-4345-8f78-562c7adf6efd" label="COR-2273" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2273/brain-nightly-memory-compaction-loop-merge-revise-retire" /> (nightly compaction, the storage-side fix) — recall-time collapse covers whatever compaction has not merged yet.
2. **No recency signal in recall:** the 90-day half-life recency weighting exists but only on `query` (`internal/cli/internal/retrieval/recency.go:66`, `retrieve.go:189`); `recall` never applies it. Add a default recency prior to recall.
3. **Flat +4 closed-negative bonus:** `facts_bm25.go:202-214` adds +4 to any closed-negative fact on any match, \~17% of the corpus, regardless of relevance. A recorded eval also found topically-similar closed-negatives out-competing the decision fact. Drop or justify the bonus.

## Constraint

Every ranking change goes through the offline eval harness (`memories eval`) before landing — recorded precedent: topic-specific bonuses were removed after a flat 23-task comparison; semantic reranking was rejected after it dropped the solving fact out of the top 6. No embedder reinstatement (recorded decision, trail #278/#416).

## Acceptance

* Eval results per change (hit rate, reciprocal rank, provenance recall) attached; regressions blocked.

Eval runs a held-out task set through a selected retriever and reports, per task and

			--judge --judge-source-matches to replace source-overlap proxy credit with

  entire-brain memories eval --tasks <file> [flags]

content.content:
eval-gen turns the brain into a self-labeled benchmark: each captured session
	becomes a task (its opening user request), and the facts whose provenance points
	back to that session are provenance/silver labels. These labels are useful for
	recall-oriented measurement, but hand labels or --refine are still required
	before precision/recall release claims. Each task is tagged with a query-type
	stratum (code/convention/howto/concept). Emits a tasks.json consumable by
	'facts eval --tasks'.

	--source sessions emits tasks directly from exported sessions, including sessions
	with zero distilled facts. Those tasks have source anchors but no relevance labels,
	so use --judge or human labels before making relevance claims.

	--refine judge-filters each task's provenance label set with the agent, keeping
only facts genuinely relevant to the request — trading the recall-oriented "every
session fact" labels for precision-clean ones (verdicts cached for reuse).

Usage:
  entire-brain memories eval-gen [flags]

Flags:
      --agent string                Agent for --refine: auto, codex, claude-code, ollama, or command (default "auto")
      --agent-command stringArray   Agent command argv for --agent command
      --branch string               Limit to one branch (default: all branches with facts)
  -h, --help                        help for eval-gen
      --judge-cache string          Persist/reuse --refine verdicts at this path
      --limit int                   Cap the number of tasks, sampled evenly across strata (0 = all)
      --max-facts int               Skip broad sessions with more relevant facts than this (diffuse targets); 0 = no cap (default 30)
      --min-facts int               Minimum relevant facts for a session to become a task (default 2)
      --model string                Model for codex/claude-code/ollama refine calls
      --out string                  Write tasks JSON to this file (default: stdout)
=== compare:
eval-compare reads two 'memories eval --json' summaries over the SAME tasks (two
retrieval configs, e.g. base vs --expand) and reports, per metric, the paired
mean delta, a two-sided Student-t p-value, Cohen's d, and a Holm-Bonferroni
family-wise significance verdict. Relevance metrics require comparable
human/judge_refined proof labels unless --allow-proxy-comparison is explicit.
Task IDs must match exactly. Non-empty task-file hashes and brain manifest
hashes must match unless the corresponding override is explicit; missing hashes
leave the comparison usable for smoke but disable release_claimable metrics. Use
it to report a lift honestly instead of eyeballing two means.

Usage:
  entire-brain memories eval-compare --a <A.json> --b <B.json> [flags]

Flags:
      --a string                        Baseline eval summary JSON (memories eval --json)
      --allow-brain-manifest-mismatch   Allow comparison when non-empty eval run_config.brain_manifest_sha256 values differ
      --allow-missing-tasks             Compare only shared task ids when eval runs have missing tasks
      --allow-proxy-comparison          Allow relevance metrics to compare runs with different relevance sources
      --allow-task-hash-mismatch        Allow comparison when non-empty eval run_config.tasks_sha256 values differ
      --alpha float                     Family-wise significance level for Holm correction (default 0.05)

# Changelog

All notable changes to `entire-brain` are recorded here. The format follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/).

## [Unreleased]

### Changed

- Building from source needs Go 1.27.3 or newer (was 1.27). Brain now reads
  compact transcripts with the CLI's own `transcript` package
  (`github.com/entireio/cli` v0.13.1), whose module requires it. The source
  installer's Go check compares the patch version too (#607).

### Fixed

- The pattern corpus now reads current Codex sessions (the cli's item path,
  in cli 0.13.1 and later). A command that failed is stored as failed, with no
  exit code since the session records none, and counts in `exit_fails`. A file
  edit gives a file ref, stored relative to the repository root (taken from the
  files the session's checkpoint touched) so it links to the file's symbols.
  The indexer version moves, so the next refresh re-indexes existing
  sessions (#600).
- `recall --evidence` no longer returns harness-injected `<system-reminder>`
  text as `role: "user"` evidence. User-role strings and text blocks now go
  through the same wrapper filter as the conversation reader, so reminders,
  `Caveat:` notes and environment envelopes are skipped like system-role
  records already were. As in conversation, user text that itself starts with
  `<` is skipped too. Assistant text is unchanged (#565).
- The pattern corpus reads a Codex command's exit code only from the header

feat(recall): kind-neutral, recency-aware, family-collapsed facts ranking

Three COR-2311 changes to the shared facts ranking (recall, brief, the
facts arms), each gated on a 60-task provenance-labeled `memories eval`
A/B with paired-t + Holm:

- Drop the flat +4 closed-negative BM25 bonus. It boosted ~17% of the
  corpus on any match with no recorded rationale, and the n=15
  memory-ladder runs showed topically-similar closed-negatives
  displacing the decision fact. Eval: no regression (precision +0.002
  ns, useful/1k +0.044 ns, latency significantly better). The legacy
  lexical scorer keeps its bonus: the post-failure hook's threshold is
  calibrated to that scale.

- Default-on gentle recency prior (x1.15 fresh to x0.85 ancient, 90-day
  half-life) on matched facts. Near-duplicate facts score within ~1%, so
  this breaks stale-vs-current ties without overriding real relevance
  gaps; dateless facts stay neutral. The fused 1.5/0.3 spread was tried
  first and regressed tokens (+55, p<.001) and useful/1k (-15%), so the
  facts prior gets its own constants. Eval at the gentle spread: no
  significant change on any metric.

- Collapse related_ids families to one result: the highest-ranked member
  represents the family (its related_ids field names the alternates) and
  freed slots backfill; --all skips the collapse for store introspection.
  Covers what the nightly compaction loop (COR-2273) has not merged yet.
  Eval: relevance tie, +0.77ms mean latency.

COR-2311

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

gh pr create --base main --title "feat(recall): kind-neutral, recency-aware, family-collapsed facts ranking (COR-2311)" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Why

With memories as the only default retrieval surface (COR-2307/2308), recall-time ranking carries the whole load. The 2026-11-06 retrieval audit and the n=15 memory-ladder runs identified three defects: a flat +4 closed-negative bonus boosting ~17% of the corpus on any match, no recency signal in recall, and related_ids near-duplicates surfacing as separate results. Linear: COR-2311. Trail: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2821/changes/entire-brain/500

## What changed

All three changes act in the shared facts ranking (`rankFacts`), so recall, brief, and the facts eval arms behave identically:

- **Closed-negative bonus dropped** (`facts_bm25.go`). Kind no longer affects ranking and never creates a match. The legacy lexical scorer keeps its bonus: the post-failure hook's threshold is calibrated to that scale.
- **Gentle default-on recency prior** (`facts_query.go`, `retrieval/recency.go`): ×1.15 (fresh) to ×0.85 (ancient), 90-day half-life, applied only to already-matched facts; dateless facts stay neutral. Near-duplicates score within ~1%, so this breaks stale-vs-current ties without overriding real relevance gaps.
- **related_ids family collapse** (`facts_query.go`): the highest-ranked member represents the family, its `related_ids` field names the alternates, freed slots backfill. `--all` skips the collapse for store introspection. Covers what the nightly compaction loop (COR-2273) has not merged yet.

## Validation

Each change gated on a 60-task provenance-labeled `memories eval` run (same tasks file, same store manifest), compared with `eval-compare` (paired-t, Holm α=0.05):

| step | precision Δ | useful/1k Δ | tokens Δ | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base → drop bonus | +0.002 ns | +0.044 ns | −20 (p=.049, ns after Holm) | pass, latency significantly better |
| drop bonus → +recency (full 1.5/0.3 spread) | −0.005 ns | −0.078 (p=.016) | **+55 (p<.001)** | **rejected**, retuned |
| drop bonus → +gentle recency +collapse | 0.000 tie | −0.012 ns | +18 ns | pass |

The full fused-recency spread demoted old-but-relevant facts, not just stale duplicates; the facts prior gets its own gentler constants with the measurement recorded in the code comment. Caveat: this benchmark's tasks come from historical sessions, so it cannot reward recency, only price it — the prior's value case is the stale-vs-current tie-break; its measured cost at the gentle spread is statistically zero.

Unit: new `TestRankFactsKindDoesNotOutrankRelevance`, `TestRankFactsRecencyPrior`, `TestRankFactsCollapsesRelatedPairs`; full `./internal/cli`, `./internal/cli/command/...`, `./internal/cli/internal/retrieval`, `./factmerge` suites pass; `gofmt -s` and `go vet` clean. Eval artifacts (tasks + 4 run summaries) in the workspace `.context/cor2311/`.

## Notes

- Collapse is greedy in rank order: a chain A–B, B–C with A ranked first keeps A and C. Pairs (the measured case, ~1,910 records) collapse fully.
- `query --recency` (fused, opt-in, 1.5/0.3) is unchanged; a query opting in applies both weights to facts.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

cd /Users/evisdrenova/conductor/workspaces/entire-brain/san-jose && gh pr create --base main --title "feat(recall): kind-neutral, recency-aware, family-collapsed facts ranking (COR-2311)" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Why

With memories as the only default retrieval surface (COR-2307/2308), recall-time ranking carries the whole load. The 2026-11-06 retrieval audit and the n=15 memory-ladder runs identified three defects: a flat +4 closed-negative bonus boosting ~17% of the corpus on any match, no recency signal in recall, and related_ids near-duplicates surfacing as separate results. Linear: COR-2311. Trail: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2821/changes/entire-brain/500

## What changed

All three changes act in the shared facts ranking (`rankFacts`), so recall, brief, and the facts eval arms behave identically:

- **Closed-negative bonus dropped** (`facts_bm25.go`). Kind no longer affects ranking and never creates a match. The legacy lexical scorer keeps its bonus: the post-failure hook's threshold is calibrated to that scale.
- **Gentle default-on recency prior** (`facts_query.go`, `retrieval/recency.go`): ×1.15 (fresh) to ×0.85 (ancient), 90-day half-life, applied only to already-matched facts; dateless facts stay neutral. Near-duplicates score within ~1%, so this breaks stale-vs-current ties without overriding real relevance gaps.
- **related_ids family collapse** (`facts_query.go`): the highest-ranked member represents the family, its `related_ids` field names the alternates, freed slots backfill. `--all` skips the collapse for store introspection. Covers what the nightly compaction loop (COR-2273) has not merged yet.

## Validation

Each change gated on a 60-task provenance-labeled `memories eval` run (same tasks file, same store manifest), compared with `eval-compare` (paired-t, Holm α=0.05):

| step | precision Δ | useful/1k Δ | tokens Δ | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base → drop bonus | +0.002 ns | +0.044 ns | −20 (p=.049, ns after Holm) | pass, latency significantly better |
| drop bonus → +recency (full 1.5/0.3 spread) | −0.005 ns | −0.078 (p=.016) | **+55 (p<.001)** | **rejected**, retuned |
| drop bonus → +gentle recency +collapse | 0.000 tie | −0.012 ns | +18 ns | pass |

The full fused-recency spread demoted old-but-relevant facts, not just stale duplicates; the facts prior gets its own gentler constants with the measurement recorded in the code comment. Caveat: this benchmark's tasks come from historical sessions, so it cannot reward recency, only price it — the prior's value case is the stale-vs-current tie-break; its measured cost at the gentle spread is statistically zero.

Unit: new `TestRankFactsKindDoesNotOutrankRelevance`, `TestRankFactsRecencyPrior`, `TestRankFactsCollapsesRelatedPairs`; full `./internal/cli`, `./internal/cli/command/...`, `./internal/cli/internal/retrieval`, `./factmerge` suites pass; `gofmt -s` and `go vet` clean. Eval artifacts (tasks + 4 run summaries) in the workspace `.context/cor2311/`.

## Notes

- Collapse is greedy in rank order: a chain A–B, B–C with A ranked first keeps A and C. Pairs (the measured case, ~1,910 records) collapse fully.
- `query --recency` (fused, opt-in, 1.5/0.3) is unchanged; a query opting in applies both weights to facts.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

input.body:
Implemented, eval-gated per change, PR up: https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/625 · Trail: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2821/changes/entire-brain/500

All three changes act in the shared `rankFacts`, so recall and brief behave identically (acceptance item 2: related_ids pairs collapse to one primary in both; the primary's `related_ids` field names the alternates, `--all` skips the collapse).

## Eval results per change (60-task provenance-labeled pack, `eval-compare`, paired-t + Holm α=0.05)

| step | precision Δ | useful/1k Δ | tokens Δ | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base → drop closed-negative bonus | +0.002 ns | +0.044 ns | −20 ns | **pass** (latency significantly better) |
| → + recency at the fused 1.5/0.3 spread | −0.005 ns | −0.078 (p=.016) | **+55 (p<.001)** | **rejected** |
| → + gentle recency (1.15/0.85) + collapse | 0.000 tie | −0.012 ns | +18 ns | **pass** |

- The flat bonus had no recorded rationale (recall search found none) and removing it cost nothing — consistent with the recorded precedent on topic bonuses.
- The full fused recency spread regressed the benchmark: it demoted old-but-relevant facts, not just stale duplicates. The shipped prior uses its own gentle constants (±15%, 90-day half-life), which still reorders near-duplicate ties (they score within ~1%) at statistically zero cost. Caveat recorded in the PR: this benchmark's tasks are historical by construction, so it can only price recency, not reward it.
- The legacy lexical scorer's +30 closed-negative bonus is untouched: it serves only the post-failure hook, whose threshold is calibrated to that scale. Flagging it here in case the compaction/ranking follow-ups want to retire it with the hook's threshold re-measured.

Eval artifacts (tasks.json + 4 run summaries) in the workspace `.context/cor2311/`.

COR-2311 is implemented, gated, and shipped for review:

That rejection is recorded in Brain (`fact:06d799c0cb06bfaee45ac35f`) and in a code comment.
- **Validation**: three new unit tests; full `internal/cli`, `command/...`, `retrieval`, `factmerge` suites pass; `gofmt -s`/`go vet` clean; per-change eval tables in the PR and on the Linear issue.
- **Trail**: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2821/changes/entire-brain/500 (the trail auto-opened the PR; I filled it and marked it ready) · **PR**: https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/625 · results posted on [COR-2311](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2311/brain-recall-ranking-quality-collapse-related-ids-pairs-recency-prior).

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Monitor
tools.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

`collapseRelatedFacts` drops every active fact whose `related_ids` link to a higher-ranked result. Those facts are, by the comment's own account, related but below the merge threshold, so they are distinct and can be complementary rather than duplicates. Consider collapsing only near-identical pairs, or flagging that alternates were omitted.

content.thinking:
I'm checking the claim that collapsing can hide complementary facts with no signal. The first half is partly wrong, since the kept fact's `related_ids` already lists the absorbed ids in the JSON output. But I'm noticing that `related_ids` also lists related facts that were never suppressed, because they simply didn't match the query, so that field alone doesn't prove anything was hidden.

I'm now weighing how weak `related_ids` is as a signal, since it lists related facts whether or not they were actually suppressed. The ticket asked for alternates to be listed, and my implementation only implicitly does that, so the cleaner fix is to emit explicit suppressed ids, though `rankFacts` would need to return extra data, which ripples through its signature.

I'm weighing whether to record the suppressed ids explicitly: adding them to the recall JSON would mean recall reaching into the ranker's internals, while putting a `collapsed_ids` field on the stored record risks it leaking into a write path if a ranked record is ever persisted back out.

I'm weighing whether to keep the collapse inside `rankFacts` and annotate the kept record, or to demote the suppressed facts to the end of the list rather than dropping them. Demotion would stop the family duplicates from crowding the top results without hiding anything outright.

I've settled on the response: I'll lean on the eval tie as evidence that nothing measurable was lost, and note that the recency prior usually keeps the current fact as the family winner. For the signal itself, I'm inclined toward something cleaner than a transient field on the storage record, though that means weighing the cost to the ranker's signature.

I'm weighing whether to expose the suppressed ids explicitly, perhaps through a second rank function that returns the collapse map that recall and brief could use, while the injected dependency stays unchanged.

I'm weighing whether to build explicit alternates plumbing now, but the finding is medium severity at low confidence, and the eval showed no measurable precision loss, so I'll hold off. I'll acknowledge the complementary-pair risk and note the alternates plumbing as the upgrade path if real misses appear, since the compaction work should shrink this class over time anyway.

I'm settling on keeping the collapse as it is and leaving the explicit alternates plumbing for later. For complementary pairs, `related_ids` already names the suppressed sibling, so the signal is there in the common case, and I'll note the upgrade path if real misses show up.

I'm going to leave the collapse as it is and skip the explicit alternates plumbing for now. Before I reply on the finding, I'll check which reply and resolve options the finding command supports. The recall text output probably doesn't show `related_ids` at all, but agents use `--json`, so that's fine.

The complementary-facts risk in the collapse is a real design tension, flagged at 0.45 and non-blocking. I'm responding to that finding now rather than adding plumbing, since the eval showed a precision tie and the related_ids link already names the suppressed sibling.

the network is not allowed means the sandbox blocked it, not that the user

content.content:
### Changed

- Facts ranking (recall, brief, the facts arms) changed in three ways
  (COR-2311). The flat closed-negative score bonus is gone: it boosted ~17% of
  the corpus on any match and let topically-similar closed-negatives displace
  the decision fact; kind no longer affects ranking. A gentle recency prior
  (±15%, 90-day half-life) now applies by default: it breaks stale-vs-current
  ties between near-duplicate facts and leaves dateless facts neutral. Facts
  cross-linked via `related_ids` collapse to one result — the highest-ranked
  member represents the family, its `related_ids` field names the alternates,
  and the freed slots backfill; `--all` skips the collapse. Each change was
  gated on a 60-task provenance-labeled `memories eval` comparison with no
  significant relevance regression.

- Building from source needs Go 1.27.3 or newer (was 1.27). Brain now reads

Description:
Three eval-gated changes to the shared facts ranking. The flat +4 closed-negative BM25 bonus is removed (kind no longer affects ranking). A gentle default-on recency prior (x1.15..x0.85, 90-day half-life) breaks stale-vs-current ties; the full fused spread was tried first and rejected for regressing tokens and useful/1k. Facts cross-linked via related_ids collapse to one result with backfill; --all skips the collapse. Every change compared on a 60-task provenance-labeled memories eval with paired-t + Holm; no significant relevance regression. Linear: https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2311

{"id":"COR-2311","uuid":"3f94fa5e-4145-45b0-b9b8-c657a3b766b5","title":"Brain: recall ranking quality — collapse related_ids pairs, recency prior, drop flat closed-negative bonus","description":"**Repo:** entireio/entire-brain · **Phase C of the memories-only retrieval decision** (see <issue id="e540d772-0613-4636-a0e3-137441d4668b" label="COR-2307" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2307/brain-brief-precedent-section-from-fact-provenance-anchors-not-history" />)

## Why

With memories as the only default retrieval surface, recall-time ranking quality carries the whole load. The 2026-11-06 retrieval audit found three concrete issues:

1. **Unresolved near-duplicates reach recall:** when distill judges two facts related below the old confidence threshold, both stay active cross-linked via `related_ids` (`factmerge/merge.go:40-46`). \~1,910 active records carry `related_ids`; pairs surface as separate results. Collapse linked facts into one result at recall time (newest or highest-scored wins, others listed as alternates). Complementary to <issue id="e6be68d8-58ee-4345-8f78-562c7adf6efd" label="COR-2273" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2273/brain-nightly-memory-compaction-loop-merge-revise-retire" /> (nightly compaction, the storage-side fix) — recall-time collapse covers whatever compaction has not merged yet.
2. **No recency signal in recall:** the 90-day half-life recency weighting exists but only on `query` (`internal/cli/internal/retrieval/recency.go:66`, `retrieve.go:189`); `recall` never applies it. Add a default recency prior to recall.
3. **Flat +4 closed-negative bonus:** `facts_bm25.go:202-214` adds +4 to any closed-negative fact on any match, \~17% of the corpus, regardless of relevance. A recorded eval also found topically-similar closed-negatives out-competing the decision fact. Drop or justify the bonus.

## Constraint

Every ranking change goes through the offline eval harness (`memories eval`) before landing — recorded precedent: topic-specific bonuses were removed after a flat 23-task comparison; semantic reranking was rejected after it dropped the solving fact out of the top 6. No embedder reinstatement (recorded decision, trail #278/#416).

## Acceptance

* Eval results per change (hit rate, reciprocal rank, provenance recall) attached; regressions blocked.
* related_ids pairs collapse to one primary result in recall and brief.","priority":{"value":0,"name":"No priority"},"url":"https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2311/brain-recall-ranking-quality-collapse-related-ids-pairs-recency-prior","gitBranchName":"evis/cor-2311-brain-recall-ranking-quality-collapse","createdAt":"2026-11-09T04:57:56.514Z","updatedAt":"2026-11-10T18:32:44.098Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":"2026-11-10T18:32:44.071Z","startedAt":"2026-11-10T05:13:41.995Z","canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Done","statusType":"completed","labels":[],"attachments":[{"id":"2b33b6f8-1e07-46bb-98dd-78cefb1379f8","title":"feat(recall): kind-neutral, recency-aware, family-collapsed facts ranking (COR-2311)","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/625"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Evis Drenova","createdById":"bd1c458e-3bb3-4d0c-8ad7-e36f19afc156","assignee":"Evis Drenova","assigneeId":"bd1c458e-3bb3-4d0c-8ad7-e36f19afc156","team":"Core","teamId":"894690b6-2173-4cbe-abd3-6e7ea5ff5bb9"}

{"id":"COR-2309","uuid":"f0a7ef73-6535-4cb4-99af-811045ffe8a6","title":"Brain: memory-ladder parity gate — memories-only brief must match plain session search","description":"**Repo:** entireio/entire-brain · **Validates:** <issue id="e540d772-0613-4636-a0e3-137441d4668b" label="COR-2307" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2307/brain-brief-precedent-section-from-fact-provenance-anchors-not-history" /> + <issue id="42fefac0-46c9-4341-8538-f9c3a4b3958b" label="COR-2308" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2308/brain-remove-history-search-and-the-raw-scan-from-briefs-default-path" />

## Why

The last memory-ladder benchmark (n=3, one closed-negative question, one repo, Sonnet) recovered a recorded decision 0/3 via brief (1/3 strict guide) while plain session search recovered it 3/3 verbatim. The recorded root cause was "brief layout + wrong guide command, not retrieval failure", marked revisit after entire-brain#335. With history search removed from brief's default path (<issue id="42fefac0-46c9-4341-8538-f9c3a4b3958b" label="COR-2308" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2308/brain-remove-history-search-and-the-raw-scan-from-briefs-default-path" />), the memories path has no safety net — parity with plain session search is the bar it must meet.

## Work

1. Confirm the two recorded defects (brief layout, wrong guide command) are fixed on main; fix any remainder.
2. Re-run the memory-ladder benchmark against the memories-only brief (<issue id="e540d772-0613-4636-a0e3-137441d4668b" label="COR-2307" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2307/brain-brief-precedent-section-from-fact-provenance-anchors-not-history" />/2308 branches): decision-recovery must match plain session search on the ladder question set. Widen beyond n=3 if the harness allows — n=3 on one repo is thin evidence either way.
3. If parity fails: the remedy is fixing distill coverage or ranking (see the distill-coverage and ranking issues), not reinstating default history search. Record failures as distill/ranking bugs with the specific missed content.

## Acceptance

* Benchmark results attached to this issue: memories-only brief vs plain session search, per question.
* Parity reached, or concrete distill/ranking bugs filed for each miss.","priority":{"value":0,"name":"No priority"},"url":"https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2309/brain-memory-ladder-parity-gate-memories-only-brief-must-match-plain","gitBranchName":"evis/cor-2309-brain-memory-ladder-parity-gate-memories-only","createdAt":"2026-11-09T04:57:28.878Z","updatedAt":"2026-11-10T04:59:15.062Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":"2026-11-10T04:59:15.044Z","startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Done","statusType":"completed","labels":[],"attachments":[],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Evis Drenova","createdById":"bd1c458e-3bb3-4d0c-8ad7-e36f19afc156","assignee":"Evis Drenova","assigneeId":"bd1c458e-3bb3-4d0c-8ad7-e36f19afc156","team":"Core","teamId":"894690b6-2173-4cbe-abd3-6e7ea5ff5bb9"}
